children: The Food and Drug Administration and Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy will convene a public workshop this month to examine one of the most difficult questions in rare disease development: how to generate reliable evidence when the number of available patients makes conventional clinical trials difficult or impossible.

The “RISE to the Challenge: Statistical Considerations for Rare Disease Clinical Investigations” meeting is scheduled for Sept. 29 from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. ET. The hybrid event will be held at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C.

According to a draft agenda, the workshop will explore how researchers can tailor the design, conduct and analysis of studies without sacrificing the scientific rigor needed to determine whether a drug or medical device works.

For biotech investors who believe promising rare disease programs have been unfairly penalized for failing to meet clinical standards designed for much larger patient populations, the workshop could signal a more workable regulatory path.

Rare disease developers frequently face practical and ethical barriers to conventional randomized trials. Eligible patients may number in the dozens rather than thousands. Some diseases progress rapidly, while others primarily affect children. Patients and families also may resist joining a study if they could receive a placebo instead of an experimental treatment.

Those constraints have led the FDA to accept single-arm studies, natural-history comparisons, surrogate endpoints and other unconventional forms of evidence in some rare disease programs. They have also fueled long-running arguments about whether regulatory flexibility can go too far.

Exondys 51 became a defining example after the FDA granted accelerated approval in 2016 for a subset of patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The decision relied on increased production of dystrophin as a surrogate endpoint, even though agency reviewers questioned whether the relatively small increase was reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit.
FDA leadership ultimately approved the treatment over those internal objections, according to the agency’s own regulatory review documents.

title: FDA, Duke-Margolis workshop to examine evidence standards for rare diseases
